tagline.text: Mountain caves in Ibaloi country where fire-dried ancestors rest

image.credit: Viktor Pinchuk / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A resting place for "fire mummies" — bodies the Ibaloi people of the Benguet highlands dried with fire and smoke centuries ago and laid in pine coffins. The nationally protected Timbac Cave, the bone-filled Opdas Cave, and a branch of the National Museum together reveal a burial tradition rarely seen elsewhere in the Philippines.
Kabayan is a mountain town in Benguet province, about
3–4 hours

up a mountain road northeast of Baguio, set in a broad valley along the Agno River. It's said to be the land where the Ibaloi people first settled, and it also borders Mount Pulag, the Philippines' third-highest peak. What brought this village to the world's attention are the centuries-old mummies kept in rock crevices and caves on the surrounding slopes.

The Ibaloi are among the few peoples in the Philippines known to have mummified their dead. According to tradition, a person nearing death was given salty water to drink; once they had passed, the body was washed, seated upright, and dried slowly over a fire for a long period. Tobacco smoke was blown into the mouth to dry the body from within, and herbs were applied to the skin. The finished mummy was placed in a coffin carved from a single pine log and laid in a cave or rock shelter — hence the common name "Fire Mummies."
The mummies are generally thought to date from around
, though some argue they're considerably older. The Philippine government declared the Kabayan Mummy Caves a National Cultural Treasure in
, and in

the World Monuments Fund placed them on its list of the 100 Most Endangered Sites. After a series of lootings and thefts in the 1970s, the National Museum opened a branch in the village to help protect the artifacts.

Kabayan is less a tourist attraction than sacred ground where ancestors are honored. The mummies are still family and forebears to local residents, so visitors are expected to stay quiet and respectful. It's a place worth recommending to travelers more interested in Cordillera mountain peoples' views on death and ancestry than in flashy sightseeing, and to anyone combining a Mount Pulag climb with a trip into the Benguet backcountry.
The site that houses the best-preserved mummies, it lies partway up Mount Timbac at an elevation of about
. However, to keep the mummies from deteriorating quickly, the National Museum has kept the cave sealed since
, so you can no longer see the mummies inside. See the mummies at the National Museum Kabayan branch, and think of the Timbac mountain trail as a place to go and enjoy the highland scenery.

blocks.title: The collective burial cave at Opdas

children.text: Close to town, Opdas Cave holds the skulls and bones of people from centuries past, stacked on rock shelves. A village elder discovered it in the early 1970s, and the same family still cares for it and honors their ancestors there today.
A small museum that opened in
, displaying one mummy along with Ibaloi and Kalanguya tools, ornaments, and coffins from daily life. Stopping here before visiting the mummy caves makes the experience much easier to understand.

A burial site where a coffin was set into a hollowed-out boulder, showing that the Ibaloi used not just caves but rock itself as a tomb. The path there passes terraced vegetable gardens and village scenery.

The Halsema Highway, which runs through the highest stretch of road in the Philippines, is famous for its endless ridgelines above the clouds and terraced vegetable farms. The turnoff to Timbac Cave branches off this road.
The Kabayan valley also grows Arabica coffee and a native red rice. Local beans or red rice from a shop in town make good souvenirs.

The Timbac Cave has been sealed since

, so chartering a vehicle from Baguio for a day trip to see the mummies is not recommended. Before you set out, check with the National Museum Kabayan branch for news of a reopening, and while the seal continues you might swap the second morning for a drive toward Mount Pulag or a look at the Atok highlands.
Baguio-bound buses such as Victory Liner and Genesis leave frequently from Cubao, Pasay, and elsewhere in Manila. It takes about
4–6 hours
and the fare is about
depending on class. To catch the first bus to Kabayan, it's best to arrive in Baguio the day before and stay overnight.

Vans and buses to Kabayan depart from around the Dangwa terminal in Baguio town or the Slaughterhouse terminal on Magsaysay Avenue. Vans leave from early morning as they fill up, while buses run only a few times a day (usually morning to noon). The trip along the Ambuklao road takes about
3–5 hours
, for a fare of around
Return trips also cluster in the morning, so be sure to confirm departure times locally the day before.

Timbac Cave sits on a narrow mountain road branching off around the 55km mark of the Halsema Highway, making it hard to reach by public transport. Renting a vehicle with a driver in Kabayan town or Baguio is the practical option, at about
round trip. Given the narrow, steep road, a 4x4 or a driver who knows the area well is recommended.
From the trailhead on the Halsema Highway side to Timbac Cave is about
6km
on foot, roughly
2 hours
. Walking up from Kabayan town involves an elevation gain of over 1,000m, making for a tough
5–7 hour
hike.
The nearest international airport is Clark International Airport (CRK); from there, take a bus to Baguio, about
3–4 hours
, then transfer to a Kabayan-bound vehicle.
Kabayan sits at about
elevation, keeping it cool year-round. In the
November–April
dry season, light rainfall makes for easy mountain travel and clear skies.
December–February
in particular sees nighttime and dawn temperatures drop to
, and it's even colder around Mount Timbac above 2,000m elevation. Be sure to bring a warm jacket.
May–October
is the rainy season, and typhoons combined with the monsoon in
July–September

especially often bring landslides that block the Ambuklao road and the Halsema Highway. Rain also makes the stairs and dirt paths to Timbac Cave very slippery. Around November 1, All Souls' Day, access may be restricted as residents visit ancestors' graves and caves to hold rites.

Kabayan town (the Poblacion) has only a handful of simple lodges and homestays, at about

a night. Many lack hot water and heating, so warm clothes and a sleeping bag liner are worth packing. Rooms are limited, so call ahead during holidays or when Mount Pulag climbers crowd the area. If you'd rather stay somewhere more comfortable, you can also base yourself in Baguio and visit by chartered vehicle on a day trip.

The food here is simple mountain-village fare. Dishes made with highland-grown cabbage, carrots, and potatoes are common, and local specialties include etag, salted and smoked pork, rice cooked from native red rice, and Benguet Arabica coffee. Most restaurants in town close early, so plan to have dinner promptly, and pack plenty of snacks and water for your day at Timbac Cave.
On arriving in Kabayan, register first as a visitor at the tourism desk near the municipal hall or the police station. Guides and cave caretakers are also arranged there.
You can only enter the mummy caves once a caretaker unlocks them. If you haven't contacted one in advance, they may not be available and you could miss out on seeing the mummies.
The museum is generally open only on weekday daytime hours. Check the National Museum's Kabayan branch's official page for the current days and hours.
The town has almost no working ATMs. Bring plenty of cash from Baguio.
The mountain drive is long with many curves, so bring motion-sickness medicine.
The stairs at Timbac Cave are steep and narrow. Wear sneakers or hiking shoes with good grip.
Combining this with a Mount Pulag climb makes for an efficient route through the Benguet backcountry. Mount Pulag requires advance booking and an orientation, so prepare for that separately.
Phone signal is weak in many areas. Save an offline map and your driver's contact number in advance.
Since
the National Museum has been renovating Site 1, which houses the female mummies, at a cost of about
, and has at times shown the exhibits in a temporary building in town. Check the exhibit location and whether it can be viewed by phone or on the museum's Facebook page before you go.

The mummies and remains are residents' ancestors and a national cultural treasure. Never touch them or the coffins, and follow the rules wherever flash photography or photography itself is prohibited. Damaging or removing artifacts is punishable by law.
Don't talk loudly or laugh inside the caves, and don't eat food there. Keeping a respectful manner is basic courtesy.
Don't seek out or enter unauthorized caves or rock tombs. Always register first and move with a guide.
Landslide and rockfall risk is high during the rainy season. Postpone mountain travel on days with heavy rain.
Weather changes suddenly and turns cold above 2,000m elevation. Bring waterproof and warm outerwear.
Admission and guide fees change often. Check the latest notice and pay only the set rate.

to preserve the mummies, and since a
